readme:
# City Building Permits Scraper

Get building permits from the public open-data portals of five large US cities, in one common format: Chicago, New York City, Los Angeles, San Francisco and Austin. Each city publishes its permits in its own layout. This actor reads them from the city portals and maps them into the same fields, so you can compare cities or load them into one table.

## What you can do with it

- Find new construction, renovation and demolition permits issued in a date range.
- Build lists of contractors and applicants active in a city, with license numbers where the city publishes them.
- Filter by permit type (for example "demolition" or "electrical") and by minimum project cost.
- Keep every original field of the city record in the `raw` object, so nothing the city publishes is lost.

All data comes from each city's public open-data portal. The actor reads the same records you can see on the portal and adds no data of its own.

## Supported cities

| Input value | City | Portal | Date used for filters |
|-------------|------|--------|-----------------------|
| `chicago` | Chicago | data.cityofchicago.org (Building Permits) | issue date |
| `nyc` | New York City | data.cityofnewyork.us (DOB NOW: Build, Approved Permits) | issue date |
| `la` | Los Angeles | data.lacity.org (Building Permits Issued from 2020 to Present) | issue date |
| `sf` | San Francisco | data.sf.gov (Building Permits) | issue date |
| `austin` | Austin | data.austintexas.gov (Issued Construction Permits) | issue date |

Results come newest first. An empty input (`{}`) runs a small demo: Chicago, 5 permits.

## Input

| Field | Type | Description | Default |
|-------|------|-------------|---------|
| `cities` | string[] | One or more of `chicago`, `nyc`, `la`, `sf`, `austin`. A comma separated string also works. | `["chicago"]` |
| `dateFrom` | string | Only permits issued on or after this date, `YYYY-MM-DD`. | none |
| `dateTo` | string | Only permits issued on or before this date, `YYYY-MM-DD`. | none |
| `permitTypes` | string[] | Keep permits whose type contains one of these words, ignoring case. Each city names its types differently. | all types |
| `minEstimatedCost` | number | Keep permits with an estimated or reported cost of at least this amount in USD. A numeric string also works. | none |
| `maxResults` | integer | Maximum permits for each selected city, 1 to 5000. A numeric string also works. | 100 (5 in the demo) |

Example:

```json
{
  "cities": ["chicago", "nyc"],
  "dateFrom": "2026-10-01",
  "permitTypes": ["demolition", "new construction"],
  "minEstimatedCost": 100000,
  "maxResults": 200
}
```

Notes on filters:

- Date and permit type filters are applied by the city portal.
- The cost filter is applied by the portal for Chicago, Los Angeles and San Francisco when the portal accepts it. For New York City and Austin, and whenever the portal does not accept it, the filter is applied after reading, and the actor looks at the 2000 newest permits that match your other filters. Permits without a cost are left out when a minimum cost is set.
- Austin publishes the total job valuation for only some permits. When it is missing, the actor adds up the building, electrical, mechanical, plumbing and medical gas valuations if they are published.

## Output

One row per permit. Fields that a city does not publish are `null`.

| Field | Description |
|-------|-------------|
| `city`, `cityName` | City code and name |
| `source` | Portal host and dataset id |
| `permitId` | Permit number as the city publishes it |
| `sourceRowId` | Row identifier inside the city dataset |
| `permitType`, `permitSubType`, `workType` | Type, sub type or class, and type of work, as published. Chicago has a `work_type` column, but it is blank for many permits, mostly newer ones, so `workType` and `workTypes` are often empty there. |
| `workDescription` | Work description text |
| `status` | Permit status |
| `issueDate`, `applicationDate`, `approvalDate`, `expirationDate` | Dates as `YYYY-MM-DD` |
| `address`, `zip` | Street address of the work and ZIP code |
| `latitude`, `longitude` | Coordinates as numbers |
| `estimatedCost`, `reportedCost` | Costs in USD as numbers. Chicago publishes a reported cost, San Francisco both an estimated and a revised cost, the other cities an estimated cost. |
| `currency` | Always `USD` |
| `contractorName`, `contractorLicense` | First contractor business listed and its license number when published |
| `applicantBusinessName`, `applicantLicense` | Applicant business and license when published |
| `ownerBusinessName` | Owner business name when published |
| `contractors` | All contractor businesses on the permit: `role`, `name`, `licenseNumber`, `phone`, `address`, `city`, `state`, `zip` |
| `permitUrl` | Link to the permit page. Only Austin publishes a link field in its dataset, so only Austin rows have it. It is `null` for Chicago, New York City, Los Angeles and San Francisco, whose datasets have no per-permit link. |
| `scrapedAt` | ISO 8601 UTC time of collection |
| `raw` | All original fields of the city record |

Sample row (New York City, `raw` shortened):

```json
{
  "city": "nyc",
  "cityName": "New York City",
  "source": "data.cityofnewyork.us dataset rbx6-tga4",
  "permitId": "B00293526-I1-FN",
  "permitType": "Construction Fence",
  "permitSubType": "Renewal Permit Without Changes",
  "workDescription": "Temporary Construction Fence",
  "status": "Permit Issued",
  "issueDate": "2026-11-04",
  "approvalDate": "2021-08-18",
  "expirationDate": "2026-12-31",
  "address": "2134 OCEAN PARKWAY, Brooklyn",
  "zip": "11223",
  "latitude": 40.597029,
  "longitude": -73.965334,
  "estimatedCost": 5000,
  "currency": "USD",
  "contractorName": "MNC GENERAL CONTR CORP",
  "contractorLicense": "028630",
  "contractors": [
    {
      "role": "GC",
      "name": "MNC GENERAL CONTR CORP",
      "licenseNumber": "028630",
      "address": "1711 GRAVESEND NECK RD, 3RD FL"
    }
  ],
  "scrapedAt": "2026-11-06T09:59:35Z",
  "raw": { "work_type": "Construction Fence", "bin": "3181927" }
}
```

## Run outcomes

| Situation | Exit code | Status message |
|-----------|-----------|----------------|
| Permits found | 0 | Delivered N permits. |
| No permit matches the filters | 0 | No permits found for these filters. Nothing was charged. |
| Max total charge reached | 0 | Stopped at the max charge limit. N permits delivered. |
| Every request refused, no rows | 1 | Describes the refusal; retry later. |
| Input that cannot be read | 1 | Invalid input, with a hint. |

## Pricing

Pay per event:

| Event | When it is charged | Price |
|-------|--------------------|-------|
| `actor-start` | Once per run, after the first permit row has been delivered. A run that delivers nothing is not charged. | $0.001 |
| `permit-result` | Per permit row delivered. | $0.0025 ($2.50 per 1,000) |

If you set a maximum total charge for the run, rows stop when the next row would exceed it, and the run ends with the status "Stopped at the max charge limit. N permits delivered."

## FAQ

**Where does the data come from?**
From each city's public open-data portal. The portal name and dataset id are in the `source` field of every row.

**How fresh is it?**
As fresh as the city makes it. Most portals update daily. A permit appears after the city publishes it.

**Why do some fields stay empty?**
The cities publish different columns. For example, Chicago has no ZIP code for the work site, Los Angeles and San Francisco list no contractors in these datasets, and Austin has coordinates for only part of its permits. Empty fields are `null`.

**Are names of individuals included?**
Contractor and applicant businesses are included as published. Names of owners, individual applicants and other individual contacts are left out of the `raw` object. Chicago contact names are kept only for contractor roles.

**How many rows can I get?**
Up to 5000 per city and run. For bigger exports, split the run by date range.

**Why is my result smaller than maxResults?**
The filters matched fewer permits than you asked for, or the city dataset has fewer rows in that range.

**Can I resume an interrupted run?**
Yes. Progress is saved after each batch. A run that is moved to another machine continues where it stopped and does not deliver or charge rows twice.

**Is this legal advice or an official record?**
No. Check the city portal for the official permit record before relying on a row.
